cover.headline: A century-old brand franchise turning into a launch platform for GSK's pipeline: on the street's P/E method and its own history GSK India has {{dcf.upside|chg}} upside; slow base growth and the DCF are the caution
cover.lead: GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals (GSK India) is 75% owned by GSK plc: ₹3,822 cr of FY26 revenue, more than 80% from general medicines (Augmentin, Calpol, T-Bact, Ceftum, Betnovate), the rest from India's leading private vaccine business and a young innovation portfolio (Shingrix, Nucala, Trelegy, Jemperli, Zejula; Blenrep next). It discloses no royalty to its parent, has no debt and ₹2,722 cr of net cash. Revenue grew only 5.5% a year in FY21-26, but margins rose from 20% to 34%, so EPS before one-offs more than doubled. After a fire at a contract manufacturer cut FY26 growth to 2%, Q1FY27 revenue rose 16.5%. At ₹2,769 the stock is 19% below its Jun-2025 peak and trades at 35.0x Sep-28E EPS against a 38.8x forward median since 2021, while pharma peers trade 8.2% above their own medians. The street values GSK India on **P/E** (Motilal Oswal 35x; Nirmal Bang 50x). We forecast EPS of ₹67.0 / 74.9 / 83.3 for FY27-29E, below Motilal Oswal. Applying **42x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹79.1** (the 38.8x median on EPS before one-offs × the pharma sector factor of 1.082) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹3,631; DCF ₹2,136, which says the price already capitalises a lot. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The base business is back to growth after a lost year
arguments.p: Q1FY27 standalone revenue rose 15% (9-10% underlying after a 4-5pp soft base): Augmentin +12.8%, T-Bact +17.9%, Calpol +8.1%, all gaining share (IQVIA evolution indices 101-106), and paediatric vaccines held a 26% value share. FY26 had lost more than ₹100 cr of general-medicine sales to the fire. Management guides the base business to 8-10% a year; we model +10.5% in FY27 (the lost sales return) and +8% after.

arguments.h: An innovation engine that finally moves the numbers
arguments.p: Innovative products rose from ~2% of sales a year earlier to 6% in Q4FY26 and 7% in Q1FY27: Shingrix +65% (₹100 cr+ a year), Nucala patients doubling, oncology (~₹10 cr a month) a year after launch. Blenrep (multiple myeloma), Arexvy (RSV vaccine) and bepirovirsen (hepatitis B) are next, with launch lags now 6-8 months behind the US. We model innovation at +70% / +40% / +30%, 11.2% of FY29E sales, below management's 10-15% ambition.

arguments.h: A cash machine, but the parent decides
arguments.p: Capex is ~1.4% of sales, 89-99% of profit has been paid out for four years and ₹2,755 cr of cash and liquid funds remain. ROE is ~45%. The catches: ~40% of sales is under price control, the general-medicine base grew ~5% a year for a decade, and GSK plc (75%) has used the listed company to sell land, a plant and two brands (the last to a group company), and ~₹890 cr was written off on the Vemgal plant after the Zinetac recall.

arguments.h: Valuation: fair on history, rich on cash flows
arguments.p: GSK India trades at 37.0x FY28E and 35.0x Sep-28E against a 38.8x forward median since 2021 (on EPS before one-offs), and its trailing P/E is −13.6% below its five-year median while the pharma set is 8.2% above. The house rule gives 42x and {{dcf.tp|inr}}. A DCF at an 11.3% cost of equity gives only ₹2,136; Motilal Oswal's 35x on our FY28E EPS gives ₹2,620. The upside needs earnings delivery and the market to keep paying its history.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the peak acute season, the first full quarter without supply constraints, and margins after Q1's front-loaded promotion.
Blenrep launch (guided for Q2 or Q3FY27) and Arexvy launch; first oncology access in public "CARE" accounts (management: six to eight months from May-2026).
Bepirovirsen (hepatitis B) approval: management expected marketing authorisation within FY27.
Monthly IQVIA data: Augmentin, Calpol, T-Bact share; Shingrix and Trelegy volumes.
Price policy: April-2027 WPI revision for NLEM drugs; any new NLEM list (2022's added two or three large GSK brands).
FY27 dividend (May-2027) and any special dividend; any further asset sales or related-party deals with GSK group companies.

sections.title: A 75%-owned GSK subsidiary: India's most trusted antibiotic and fever brands, the leading private vaccine business, and a young specialty portfolio

blocks.p: GSK India sells prescription medicines and vaccines in India (98.6% of revenue; exports ₹52 cr). It is 75% owned by GSK plc of the UK through four holding companies. Revenue was ₹3,822 cr in FY26 (consolidated) from three businesses. **General medicines (more than 80%)**: anti-infectives (Augmentin, the #3 brand in the Indian market and the most prescribed antibiotic; Ceftum), pain (Calpol, ~one-third of the paracetamol market), dermatology (Betnovate, T-Bact with a 57.5% share of its market, Neosporin, Tenovate, Physiogel), thyroid (Eltroxin) and vitamins (CCM, Cobadex CZS). Seven of its brands are in the market's top 100. **Vaccines**: the leading private (self-pay) paediatric vaccine business (Infanrix Hexa, Boostrix, Havrix, Varilrix, Synflorix, Priorix, Menveo, Fluarix Tetra; 26% value share) and, since 2023, adult vaccination (Shingrix, ₹100 cr+ a year). **Specialty**: respiratory biologics and inhalers (Nucala, Trelegy Ellipta) and, since Sep-2025, oncology (Jemperli, Zejula), with Blenrep (multiple myeloma) approved. General medicines are made at its own Nashik plant (334 mn packs a year) and by ~20 contract manufacturers; vaccines and specialty products are imported from GSK group companies (₹370 cr from GSK Biologicals, Belgium in FY26).

blocks.callout: **So what:** GSK India is two companies in one. The large one is a mature, cash-rich brand business in acute therapies (antibiotics, fever, skin) where it has lost share of the overall market for a decade, partly to price control and generics, partly because it is absent from cardiac and diabetes. The small one is the Indian launch pad for GSK plc's specialty pipeline, growing ~100% a year from a low base. The investment case depends on how fast the second grows and whether the first keeps growing at 7-8%.

sections.title: A century in India: two mergers, a recall, a written-off plant, land and brand sales, and a turnaround in margins

blocks.p: GSK India was incorporated in 1924 and reached its present shape through the global mergers of its parents: SmithKline Beecham's Indian business merged in from 2001 and Burroughs Wellcome (India) from 2004. Since then the listed company has mostly shrunk its asset base: it sold its Thane land to Oberoi Realty (2019), wrote off and sold the new Vemgal plant after GSK's worldwide recall of ranitidine (Zinetac) in 2019, and sold the Iodex and Ostocalcium consumer brands to GSK's consumer arm (2021-22) as GSK plc separated its consumer business (now Haleon). Each event produced a large one-off in the accounts, which is why reported EPS is a poor guide to the trend. The share count has been 16.94 cr since a 1:1 bonus in 2018.

blocks.callout: **Our read:** the listed company has been run for cash and margins, not for growth or assets, and minority holders have shared in the proceeds (₹20 and ₹60 special dividends). The structural question is how the parent splits its Indian business between the listed company and its unlisted Indian entities (GlaxoSmithKline Pharma India Pvt Ltd sold it ₹73 cr of products in FY26). So far the specialty launches have come to the listed company.

sections.title: The Indian drug market: ₹2.57 lakh crore, growing ~10% (13.5% in Q1FY27) with regulated prices; GSK sits in the acute, price-controlled part

blocks.p: India's domestic drug market was worth ₹2,565 bn at chemist prices in FY26, up 9.9% (IQVIA). It accelerated in Q1FY27 to 13.5%, "fairly balanced between volume, price, and new introductions" (GSK). Acute therapies (infections, pain, skin) are still 60% of the market, but chronic therapies (heart, diabetes) grow faster, and GSK is "conspicuous by our absence" in cardiology and diabetes (MD). Four forces matter for GSK. (1) **Price control:** medicines on the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) may raise prices only by the wholesale price index each April (+0.65% from 1-Apr-2026); about 40% of GSK India's sales are covered, and the 2022 list added "two or three of our big brands". (2) **Generics:** amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefuroxime, paracetamol and umeclidinium (Trelegy, since Apr-2025) all face dozens of copies. (3) **Vaccines:** the private paediatric market is concentrated and GSK leads it; adult vaccination is a new self-pay category. (4) **Specialty and oncology:** the fastest-growing segment (+27% in Q1FY27) but small in volume, priced at ₹10-16 lakh a course and reliant on patient-assistance and public "CARE" accounts.

blocks.callout: **So what:** GSK India plays where the Indian market is slowest and most regulated (acute, price-controlled) and, now, where it is fastest and least regulated (specialty, oncology, adult vaccines). Its blended growth will sit between the two: below the market until innovation is a meaningful share of sales.

sections.title: Does the market tailwind reach GSK India? Yes in Q1FY27, after a decade of lagging; the proof will be FY27-28

blocks.p: For years GSK India grew well below the market: revenue +5.5% a year in FY21-26 against ~9-10% for the IPM, and +1.9% in FY26 (the CMO fire). Q1FY27 broke the pattern: standalone revenue +15% against IPM growth of 13.5%, though 4-5 points came from the soft base. Underlying growth of 9-10% is close to the market for the first time in years, helped by ~4 points from innovation. Volume grew 3-3.5%, price ~6% and new introductions the rest (MD).

sections.title: General medicines: 80% of revenue, iconic acute brands gaining share, but ~5% a year growth for a decade and ~40% under price control

blocks.p: General medicines are GSK India's cash engine: more than 80% of revenue, brands prescribed by 80% of doctors who prescribe at all (AR FY26), mostly made in India at its Nashik plant and by contract manufacturers. Augmentin is the most prescribed antibiotic in India and the third-largest brand in the market; Calpol holds nearly a third of paracetamol; T-Bact 57.5% of topical mupirocin; Ceftum doubled its volumes in FY26 despite price cuts mandated in 2023. In Q1FY27 every promoted brand grew faster than its market (evolution indices 101-106). The weaknesses are the growth rate and pricing. General medicines were "more or less flat" in FY26 (3-4% underlying) because a fire at a key contract manufacturer in Apr-2025 stopped Calpol, Cobadex CZS and other products for most of the year, costing more than ₹100 cr of sales. Older tail brands and the distributed portfolio were soft in Q4FY26. Management now expects 6-8% a year for general medicines.

blocks.callout: **So what:** the brands are strong enough to hold or gain share in crowded, generic markets, which is rare. But this is a 6-8% growth business with capped pricing: ~40% of sales can raise prices only with wholesale inflation (+0.65% this year), the rest by up to 10%. We model the whole base business (general medicines plus established vaccines) at +10.5% in FY27 (the lost ₹100 cr+ returns) and +8% a year after.

sections.title: Vaccines: leader of the private paediatric market, growing double digits for six quarters; Shingrix is building adult vaccination from scratch

blocks.p: GSK India is the largest private vaccine company in India: "a GSK vaccine administered to an infant every seven seconds" (AR FY26), with a 26.1% value share of the private market (IQVIA Jun-2026) across hexavalent (Infanrix Hexa), Tdap (Boostrix), hepatitis A (Havrix), chickenpox (Varilrix), pneumococcal (Synflorix), MMR (Priorix), meningococcal (Menveo) and flu (Fluarix Tetra). Vaccines grew 11-12% in FY26 and double digits for six successive quarters (MD). The vaccines are imported from GSK Biologicals in Belgium (₹370 cr of purchases in FY26). Adult vaccination is new: Shingrix (shingles) sold ~100,000 doses (~₹70-75 cr) in calendar 2025, crossed ₹100 cr on a moving-annual basis by Q1FY27 and grew 65% in that quarter, after GSK repositioned it towards older patients with heart disease and diabetes, who are at higher shingles risk. Arexvy, an RSV vaccine for older adults, received marketing authorisation in 2026; management calls it "a new category creation" with 10-12 million affluent over-50s as the potential pool.

sections.title: Specialty and innovation: from ~2% to 7% of sales in five quarters; we model 11.2% by FY29E, management aims for 10-15%

blocks.p: GSK India's "innovation portfolio" is GSK plc's patented products launched in India in the last few years: adult vaccines (Shingrix), new respiratory (Nucala, a biologic for severe eosinophilic asthma; Trelegy Ellipta, a once-daily triple inhaler) and oncology (Jemperli for first-line endometrial cancer and Zejula for ovarian cancer, launched Sep-2025). It was ~2% of sales in Q4FY25 (like-for-like), 4% in Q1FY26, 6% in Q4FY26 and 7% in Q1FY27, when it contributed about 4 points of growth. Evidence by product: Nucala ~600 patients on treatment, 100-120 new patients a month (double a year earlier); Trelegy holds 10,000-12,000 units a month despite 10-12 generics of one of its molecules since Apr-2025; oncology treated 263 patients in Q1FY27 and is running at ~₹10 cr a month with ~45 representatives. Next: Blenrep (belantamab mafodotin, an antibody-drug conjugate for second-line multiple myeloma; 18,000 new patients a year) is approved and guided for launch in Q2 or Q3FY27; Arexvy is authorised; bepirovirsen, the first potential functional cure for chronic hepatitis B (~25% functional cure in trials; 40 mn Indians infected), is "three to four quarters away"; 26 clinical trials run in India, cutting the launch lag behind the US to 6-8 months.

blocks.callout: **So what:** this is the growth story, and it is real but early. Even at +70% / +40% / +30% (our build) innovation is only ~11% of FY29E revenue, so it adds ~3 points a year to group growth. Imported, IP-protected products carry high prices but lower gross margins than local generics and need heavy medical investment; management says it will hold, not expand, margins while it launches. The upside case is management's: 10-15% of sales in FY27-28 and ₹8,000 cr of revenue in four to five years, which needs ~13% a year.

sections.title: Dealings with GSK plc: no royalty disclosed, ₹504 cr of purchases from group companies, ₹480 cr of dividends, and a history of asset sales

blocks.p: Many Indian subsidiaries of foreign drug makers pay their parent a royalty or brand fee. GSK India's FY26 related-party note shows none: the flows are purchases, recharges, manufacturing charges and dividends. **Purchases** from GSK group companies were ₹504 cr in FY26 (₹413 cr in FY25): vaccines from GSK Biologicals, Belgium (₹370 cr), products from GlaxoSmithKline Pharma India Pvt Ltd, an unlisted GSK company in India (₹73 cr, up from ₹22 cr), and GSK Export, UK (₹16 cr). **Recharges:** GSK India recharged ₹34 cr of costs to group companies (₹166 cr in FY25, of which ₹148 cr to GSK Biologicals) and was charged ₹13.5 cr. **Dividends:** ₹480 cr to the four promoter companies in FY26 (net of tax deducted). **Asset deals:** in FY22 the Iodex and Ostocalcium brands went to GlaxoSmithKline Asia, a group company, for ₹1,649 cr with minority shareholders' approval.

blocks.callout: **Our read: GREEN on terms, AMBER on structure.** No royalty is a real plus, and the specialty launches are coming to the listed company rather than to an unlisted affiliate. But the parent controls the brands and the pipeline, decides which products are routed through the listed company or GSK Pharma India Pvt Ltd, sets the payout, and has used the listed company to sell assets to group companies. Purchases from GSK Biologicals will rise with Shingrix and Arexvy (they already exceed ₹350 cr a year), so their transfer prices matter for gross margins and for minority approval under SEBI related-party rules.

sections.title: Price control: ~40% of sales under NLEM; FY27's allowed increase is 0.65%, so growth must come from volume, mix and launches

blocks.p: India caps the prices of medicines on the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) through the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO); the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) sets a ceiling and lets it rise each April by the wholesale price index: +0.65% from 1-Apr-2026. Other medicines may rise up to 10% a year. GSK India gives three figures for its exposure: 35-38% of the portfolio (Feb-2026), "almost 40% of our business" (May-2026) and 44-45% of the general-medicine portfolio (Aug-2026). The 2022 NLEM brought two or three of its big brands under control; Ceftum took a mandated price cut in 2023 and doubled volumes since. GSK also carries a 40-year-old price-control dispute: the government's 1981-87 betamethasone price-equalisation demand (principal paid; ₹247 cr interest claim provided, ₹137 cr deposited, writ pending).

blocks.p: The moat is in trust: doctors have prescribed Augmentin, Calpol and Betnovate for decades and keep doing so at a premium to dozens of cheaper copies, and parents pay for GSK vaccines privately. Together with very low capital needs, that is why GSK India earns a return on equity of ~45% even with ₹2,755 cr of low-yielding cash. The second advantage is newer and borrowed: GSK plc now uses India as a launch market for patented products, which no domestic competitor can copy. The moat does not protect prices, and the listed company does not own its pipeline: it is licensed from a parent that also decides what to sell and to whom.

blocks.callout: **Verdict:** a genuine, if narrow, moat. The brands and vaccines justify a premium to generic-led pharma, and the pipeline access is a real option. But the base business has grown slower than the market for a decade, so the premium has to be earned by the launches.

sections.title: Revenue +5.5% a year since FY21, EPS before one-offs +17%: margins did all the work, and reported EPS was a mess of one-offs

blocks.p: GSK India's revenue (continuing operations) grew from ₹2,926 cr in FY21 to ₹3,822 cr in FY26, only 5.5% a year, about half the pace of the Indian drug market. Earnings grew three times faster: EPS before one-off items rose from ₹27.2 to ₹60.1 (17% a year). Almost all of that came from the EBITDA margin (operating profit before other income), which climbed from 20.4% to 34.3% as GSK shifted its mix away from price-controlled products, raised prices where it could, sourced more cheaply, cut ~470 jobs in FY24 (voluntary retirement) and used its field force better. Reported EPS tells a confusing story: ₹5.5 in FY20 (a write-off of the Vemgal plant), ₹100 in FY22 (the sale of the Iodex and Ostocalcium brands), ₹34.8 in FY24 (retirement-scheme costs). FY26 was a stall: revenue +1.9% because a fire at a contract manufacturer cut supplies of Calpol and other brands for most of the year, but EBITDA still rose 11%.

blocks.p: Between FY21 and FY26 GSK India added 13.8 points to its EBITDA margin. Materials and traded goods fell from 43.0% to 35.4% of revenue (7.6 points): the CFO lists three levers, a mix shift away from price-controlled products, pricing in step with peers where allowed, and cheaper sourcing for NLEM products (forward contracts, new suppliers). Employee costs fell from 21.1% to 15.9% (5.2 points) after the FY24 voluntary retirement scheme and as sales per representative rose (₹15-16 lakh a month in Q1FY27). Other expenses fell one point despite launch spending. The quarterly pattern matters for FY27: Q1 is the weakest quarter (31.5% in Q1FY27, with promotion deliberately front-loaded before the monsoon season) and Q2-Q3 the strongest (34-36%).

sections.title: Capital allocation: ~90% of profit paid out and specials after asset sales; but the Vemgal plant destroyed ~₹890 cr

blocks.p: GSK India needs little capital: one owned plant (Nashik), ~20 contract manufacturers and imported vaccines and specialty products. Capex was ₹55 cr in FY26 (₹23 cr in FY25) against ₹903 cr of operating cash flow (₹1,290 cr in FY25). It pays out almost everything: dividends were 89-99% of EPS in FY23-26 (₹57 a share for FY26, ₹966 cr, paid in Aug-2026), with special dividends when it sells assets (₹20 a share after the Thane land, ₹60 after the Iodex/Ostocalcium sale). The blemish is the Vemgal plant in Karnataka: capital work in progress reached ₹1,003 cr by Mar-2019, then the global ranitidine (Zinetac) recall removed its purpose and GSK wrote off ~₹890 cr and sold the site for ~₹180 cr. The FY22 brand sale went to a GSK group company (GlaxoSmithKline Asia, now Haleon) for ₹1,649 cr, about 6x the brands' FY21 sales of ₹273 cr; minority shareholders approved it.

blocks.callout: **The capital question.** ₹2,755 cr of cash is ~6% of GSK India's market value and earns ~5% before tax, far below the business's 45% return on equity. Cash rises by only ~₹100-250 cr a year because almost all profit goes out as dividends, three-quarters of it to GSK plc (₹480 cr in FY26 after tax deducted). We assume a 90% payout and no acquisitions. The risk is not hoarding but the parent's choices on assets: in the last seven years the listed company sold its Thane land, a plant and two brands, the last to a group company.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean accounts and good cash conversion, but frequent one-offs and ₹719 cr of tax and legal provisions to watch

bullets: **One-offs are frequent and large.** In six of the last seven years exceptional items or discontinued operations moved EPS by more than 5%: a land gain and plant write-off (FY20), more write-offs (FY21), the ₹1,314 cr brand-sale profit (FY22), a voluntary retirement scheme (FY24), property gains (FY25-26). We value and forecast on EPS before them (FY26: ₹60.1 vs ₹61.2 reported).

**Other income is 10% of profit before tax** (FY26: ₹145 cr, of which ₹136 cr from deposits and liquid funds). Screener classifies the ₹80 cr of fund gains as exceptional; they are recurring treasury income and we treat them so.
**Labour codes.** The new labour codes added ₹11.8 cr to Q3FY26 employee costs, booked as an operating cost, not an exceptional item.

**Cash conversion.** Operating cash flow was ₹903 cr in FY26 (87% of profit) after ₹319 cr of tax, lower than FY25's ₹1,290 cr because payables fell ₹139 cr and FY25 had benefited from low tax payments (₹82 cr). Before tax, cash from operations was 93% of EBITDA (Screener).

**Tax and legal provisions.** ₹546 cr of current tax liabilities (net), provisions for an old price-control dispute (₹123 cr) and indirect-tax matters (₹360 cr): ₹719 cr net of tax assets, ~₹42 a share. Contingent liabilities not provided: ₹266 cr plus ₹248 cr of disputed income tax.

**Auditor:** Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP, unmodified opinion; the only key audit matter is revenue cut-off. Sales are booked net of ₹401 cr of trade discounts and a ₹54 cr provision for expected returns.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** The accounts are conventional and conservative: no debt, no capitalised development costs, no acquisitions, and exceptional items are disclosed separately. What needs reading is outside the operating line: the history of one-offs, the treasury share of profit (which falls if payouts rise or rates fall) and the provisions for long-running tax and pricing disputes.

sections.title: Balance sheet: debt-free, ₹2,755 cr of cash and funds, and working capital funded by suppliers; watch ₹719 cr of tax and legal provisions

blocks.p: At Mar-26 GSK India had no borrowings; its only financial debt was ₹33.27 cr of leases. It held ₹2,755 cr of treasury: ₹1,102 cr of cash and short deposits, ₹262 cr of 3-12-month deposits and ₹1,391 cr in liquid mutual funds. Net cash was therefore ₹2,722 cr (~₹161 a share), before the ₹966 cr dividend paid in Aug-2026. Against that sit ₹719 cr of non-operating liabilities: net tax balances (₹546 cr of current tax liabilities less tax assets and deferred tax) and provisions for old price-control and indirect-tax disputes (₹485 cr). Their timing is unknown; we treat them as debt-like in the DCF discussion. Working capital is negative: inventory of ~124 days of cost is funded by ~154 days of supplier credit, and customers pay in ~26 days.

blocks.p: GSK India is run by a team appointed through GSK's global structure: Managing Director Bhushan Akshikar (since 2022, re-appointed in Aug-2026; 15+ years at GSK after 15 at Johnson & Johnson) and CFO Ronojit Biswas (from 1-Apr-2026, succeeding Juby Chandy). sections.title: The street: thin coverage, targets ₹2,500-3,425; both houses that disclose a method use P/E

blocks.p: Few houses publish on GSK India. sections.title: Our honest summary: a trusted franchise with a real growth option, priced near its history; the upside needs the launches to deliver

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's #2 MNC drug maker: brands doctors have trusted for decades (Augmentin, Calpol, T-Bact, Ceftum, Betnovate), the leading private vaccine business, and first access in India to GSK plc's patented pipeline (Shingrix, Nucala, Jemperli; Blenrep, Arexvy, bepirovirsen next). ROE ~45%, no debt, ₹2,722 cr of net cash, a ~2.2% dividend yield and no royalty to the parent. **What you are not buying:** pricing power (~40% of sales price-controlled), a presence in chronic therapies, a record of double-digit growth, or control over the pipeline and assets, which sit with GSK plc.

**What you are paying:** ₹2,769 is 43.9x trailing EPS, 41.4x FY27E, 37.0x FY28E and 35.0x Sep-28E: FY28E is 5% below the 38.8x forward median since 2021, while pharma peers trade 8.2% above theirs. On the street's method and our EPS (below Motilal Oswal's), the house multiple of 42x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a BUY under our rule. The DCF (₹2,136) says the opposite. The honest reading: the stock is reasonably priced against its own history and its sector only if revenue really compounds at 10%+; the history was made while margins rose 14 points, and that lever is spent.

**Biggest swing factor: the multiple.** Each 1x on the P/E is ~₹79 a share; the own-de-rating sensitivity (33.5x) would put fair value at ~₹2,650, below today's price. Each 1pp of FY28-29E EBITDA margin is ~₹2.2 of Sep-28E EPS (~₹92 a share at 42x).

head: Term
What it means
rows: Indian pharmaceutical market: sales of medicines through chemists, measured at retail prices (IQVIA)
IQVIA tracks chemist sales by brand; EI = a brand's growth ÷ its market's growth × 100 (above 100 = gaining share)
Moving annual total: sales over the latest twelve months
GSK India's established prescription brands (antibiotics, pain, dermatology, thyroid, vitamins): more than 80% of revenue
GSK plc's patented products launched in India in the last few years (Shingrix, Nucala, Trelegy, Jemperli, Zejula) as a share of sales
Contract manufacturing organisation: a third-party plant that makes products for GSK India

National List of Essential Medicines; Drug Price Control Order; National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, which caps prices of listed medicines and allows increases in line with wholesale inflation (WPI) each April
Drug Prices Equalisation Account: a 1979-87 price-control mechanism under which the government still claims money from GSK India (betamethasone)
Multinational company; here, an Indian listed subsidiary of a foreign drug maker
The controlling shareholder (GSK plc, 75.00%) / shares held by everyone else (25.00%)
A deal with a company in the same group (vaccine purchases from GSK Biologicals, the FY22 brand sale to GlaxoSmithKline Asia)
One-off gains or costs shown separately (land and brand sales, impairments, retirement schemes); discontinued operations = the profit of a business that was sold
Earnings per share from continuing operations before exceptional items, as disclosed by the company; the basis of our valuation history
A year whose EPS is a loss or below half the highest EPS of the previous three years; dropped from the forward-P/E median
An antibody that carries a cancer drug to the tumour cell (Blenrep)
Virus suppressed to undetectable levels without continuing treatment (bepirovirsen's goal)
Operating profit before depreciation, interest, tax and other income
Interest and fund gains on cash, deposits and liquid funds ÷ the balance
Share price ÷ next full fiscal year's EPS; Sep-28E EPS = half FY28E + half FY29E, the forward EPS one year from now

Enterprise value (market value less net cash) ÷ EBITDA
Discounted cash flow value; the cost of equity (11.3%) is the return shareholders require, used as the discount rate (GSK India has no debt)
Return on equity (profit ÷ shareholders' funds) / return on capital employed
